what_it_does: Running generative AI models (particularly diffusion models that create images by starting with noise and refining it) on edge devices like cameras and phones requires running a bottleneck called an autoencoder—a neural network that compresses images down to a compact representation and later decompresses them. The challenge is fitting this in a tiny chip (0.168 mm²) with minimal power while maintaining speed (8K video at 60 frames per second). The MAE chip uses a technique called line-based depth-first fusion: instead of buffering entire compressed feature maps in the fast on-chip cache, it processes data in horizontal strips, keeping only active working data on-chip. This reduces DRAM trips (energy-hungry external memory accesses) from the dominant cost down to a minor factor, while a smart global scheduling algorithm balances latency and memory bandwidth.
